formulas.name: Quadratic formula (plus root)

variables.name: root with the plus sign
variables.description: A solution of a x² + b x + c = 0. When a > 0 it is the larger root.

variables.name: coefficient of x²
variables.description: The number in front of x². It must not be zero.

variables.name: coefficient of x
variables.description: The number in front of x.

variables.name: constant term
variables.description: The number without any x.

formulas.explanation: Every quadratic equation a x² + b x + c = 0 can be solved with this formula. It comes from completing the square: divide by a, move c across, add (b/2a)² to both sides and take the square root. The ± in the full formula gives two roots; this version uses the plus sign. If the number under the root is negative there are no real roots.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it whenever a quadratic does not factorise easily, or when you want exact roots quickly.

example.story: Solve 2x² - 3x - 5 = 0 and find the root that uses the plus sign.

formulas.name: Quadratic formula (minus root)

variables.name: root with the minus sign
variables.description: A solution of a x² + b x + c = 0. When a > 0 it is the smaller root.

variables.name: coefficient of x²
variables.description: The number in front of x². It must not be zero.

variables.name: coefficient of x
variables.description: The number in front of x.

variables.name: constant term
variables.description: The number without any x.

formulas.explanation: This is the second half of the quadratic formula, taking the minus sign in front of the square root. Together with the plus root it gives both solutions of a x² + b x + c = 0. The two roots are mirror images about the axis of symmetry x = -b/(2a).
formulas.whenToUse: Use it together with the plus root to find both solutions of a quadratic equation.

example.story: Find the smaller solution of x² - 5x + 6 = 0.

formulas.name: Discriminant of a quadratic

variables.name: discriminant
variables.description: Decides how many real roots the quadratic has.

variables.name: coefficient of x²
variables.description: The number in front of x².

variables.name: coefficient of x
variables.description: The number in front of x.

variables.name: constant term
variables.description: The number without any x.

formulas.explanation: The discriminant is the expression under the square root in the quadratic formula. If D > 0 there are two different real roots, if D = 0 there is exactly one (a repeated root), and if D < 0 there are no real roots because you cannot take the square root of a negative number. Graphically it tells you whether the parabola crosses, touches or misses the x axis.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find out how many solutions a quadratic has before (or instead of) solving it, for example in questions about tangents or intersections.

example.story: How many real solutions does 3x² + 4x + 2 = 0 have?
steps: D < 0, so there are no real solutions

formulas.name: Axis of symmetry of a parabola

variables.name: x coordinate of the vertex
variables.description: Where the parabola y = a x² + b x + c turns; also the line of symmetry.

variables.name: coefficient of x²
variables.description: The number in front of x². It must not be zero.

variables.name: coefficient of x
variables.description: The number in front of x.

formulas.explanation: A parabola is symmetric about a vertical line through its turning point (vertex). That line sits exactly halfway between the two roots, which is the average of the plus and minus roots: -b/(2a). Setting the derivative 2a x + b to zero gives the same result.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the turning point, the maximum or minimum of a quadratic, or the line of symmetry when sketching a graph.

example.story: Find the line of symmetry of y = x² - 6x + 5.

formulas.name: Turning point value of a parabola

variables.name: y coordinate of the vertex
variables.description: The minimum (if a > 0) or maximum (if a < 0) value of a x² + b x + c.

variables.name: coefficient of x²
variables.description: The number in front of x². It must not be zero.

variables.name: coefficient of x
variables.description: The number in front of x.

variables.name: constant term
variables.description: The number without any x; also where the graph crosses the y axis.

formulas.explanation: Substituting x = -b/(2a) into a x² + b x + c gives the height of the vertex. This is the same as completing the square: a x² + b x + c = a(x + b/(2a))² + c - b²/(4a). The squared term is never negative, so c - b²/(4a) is the lowest value when a > 0 and the highest when a < 0.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for optimisation problems with a quadratic, such as the highest point of a thrown ball or the maximum area for a fixed fence length.

example.story: What is the minimum value of y = x² - 6x + 5?

formulas.name: Sum of the roots of a quadratic

variables.name: sum of the roots
variables.description: x₁ + x₂ for the two roots of a x² + b x + c = 0.

variables.name: coefficient of x
variables.description: The number in front of x.

variables.name: coefficient of x²
variables.description: The number in front of x². It must not be zero.

formulas.explanation: If x₁ and x₂ are the roots, the quadratic factorises as a(x - x₁)(x - x₂). Expanding gives a x² - a(x₁ + x₂)x + a x₁ x₂, and comparing with a x² + b x + c shows x₁ + x₂ = -b/a. This is one of Vieta's formulas, and it also holds for complex roots.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to check your roots, or to answer questions about the roots without finding them.

example.story: Without solving, find the sum of the roots of 2x² - 3x - 5 = 0.
steps: Check: the roots are 2.5 and -1, and 2.5 + (-1) = 1.5

formulas.name: Product of the roots of a quadratic

variables.name: product of the roots
variables.description: x₁ × x₂ for the two roots of a x² + b x + c = 0.

variables.name: constant term
variables.description: The number without any x.

variables.name: coefficient of x²
variables.description: The number in front of x². It must not be zero.

formulas.explanation: Writing the quadratic as a(x - x₁)(x - x₂) and expanding, the constant term is a x₁ x₂. Comparing with c shows that the roots multiply to c/a. A negative product means one root is positive and the other negative.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to check roots, to build a quadratic from given roots, or to reason about the signs of the roots.

example.story: Find the product of the roots of 2x² - 3x - 5 = 0.

formulas.name: Difference of two squares

variables.name: first number
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

variables.name: second number
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

formulas.explanation: Multiplying out (a + b)(a - b) gives a² - ab + ab - b², and the middle terms cancel. So a difference of two squares always factorises into a sum times a difference. It is one of the most useful factorisations in algebra.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to factorise expressions like x² - 9, to simplify fractions, or for quick mental arithmetic with numbers near a round number.

example.story: Work out 103 × 97 in your head by writing it as (100 + 3)(100 - 3).

formulas.name: Square of a sum

variables.name: first term
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

variables.name: second term
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

formulas.explanation: Squaring a sum is not the same as adding the squares: (a + b)² = (a + b)(a + b) = a² + ab + ba + b². The two middle products combine into 2ab. A picture helps: a square of side a + b splits into an a by a square, a b by b square and two a by b rectangles.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to expand brackets, to complete the square, or to square numbers like 51 quickly.

example.story: Calculate 51² without a calculator.

formulas.name: Square of a difference

variables.name: first term
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

variables.name: second term
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

formulas.explanation: This is the square of a sum with b replaced by -b. The cross term changes sign, giving -2ab, while b² stays positive because (-b)² = b².
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to expand brackets like (x - 3)², and in completing the square.

example.story: Calculate 49² without a calculator.

formulas.name: Cube of a sum

variables.name: first term
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

variables.name: second term
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

formulas.explanation: Multiplying (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² by (a + b) once more gives four terms. The coefficients 1, 3, 3, 1 are the fourth row of Pascal's triangle, which is the general pattern of the binomial theorem.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to expand (x + k)³ quickly or to recognise a perfect cube.

example.story: Calculate 11³ by splitting 11 into 10 + 1.

formulas.name: Sum of two cubes

variables.name: first number
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

variables.name: second number
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

formulas.explanation: A sum of two cubes always has (a + b) as a factor, because putting a = -b makes it zero. Dividing out that factor leaves a² - ab + b², which you can check by multiplying back.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to factorise expressions such as x³ + 8 or to simplify algebraic fractions.

example.story: Check the identity for a = 3 and b = 2.

formulas.name: Difference of two cubes

variables.name: first number
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

variables.name: second number
variables.description: Any real number or expression.

formulas.explanation: A difference of cubes always has (a - b) as a factor, because it is zero when a = b. The other factor a² + ab + b² has no real roots unless a = b = 0, so this is the complete factorisation over the real numbers.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to factorise expressions such as x³ - 27 or to find where a cubic crosses zero.

example.story: Check the identity for a = 10 and b = 2.

formulas.name: Arithmetic sequence, nth term

variables.name: nth term
variables.description: The term in position n.

variables.name: first term
variables.description: The term in position 1.

variables.name: term number
variables.description: The position in the sequence (1, 2, 3, ...).

variables.name: common difference
variables.description: The fixed amount added to get from one term to the next.

formulas.explanation: In an arithmetic sequence you add the same number d each time. To reach term n from the first term you take n - 1 steps, so you add d exactly n - 1 times. The terms lie on a straight line when plotted against n.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find any term of a sequence that goes up or down by a fixed step, or to find which position a given value has.
assumptions: the difference between consecutive terms is constant

example.story: The sequence 5, 8, 11, 14, ... continues. Which term is equal to 62?

formulas.name: Arithmetic series sum

variables.name: sum of the first n terms
variables.description: a₁ + a₂ + ... + aₙ.

variables.name: number of terms
variables.description: How many terms are added.

variables.name: first term
variables.description: The first term of the sequence.

variables.name: common difference
variables.description: The fixed step between terms.

formulas.explanation: Write the sum forwards and backwards and add the two lines: every pair of terms adds up to the same total, first plus last. There are n such pairs, which counts the sum twice, so S = n(first + last)/2. Replacing the last term by a₁ + (n - 1)d gives this form.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to add up many terms of an arithmetic sequence when you know the first term and the common difference.

example.story: Find 3 + 7 + 11 + 15 + ... for the first 15 terms.

formulas.name: Arithmetic series sum (first and last term)

variables.name: sum of the terms
variables.description: The total of all n terms.

variables.name: number of terms
variables.description: How many terms are added.

variables.name: first term
variables.description: The first term.

variables.name: last term
variables.description: The last term that is added.

formulas.explanation: The sum of an arithmetic series is the number of terms times the average of the first and last term. The story goes that young Gauss used this to add 1 to 100 in seconds: 50 pairs each adding to 101.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when you know the first and last terms, for example sums of consecutive whole numbers.

example.story: Add up all the whole numbers from 1 to 100.

formulas.name: Geometric sequence, nth term

variables.name: nth term
variables.description: The term in position n.

variables.name: first term
variables.description: The term in position 1.

variables.name: common ratio
variables.description: The fixed number each term is multiplied by.

variables.name: term number
variables.description: The position in the sequence (1, 2, 3, ...).

formulas.explanation: In a geometric sequence each term is the previous one multiplied by the same ratio r. Reaching term n takes n - 1 multiplications, which is r to the power n - 1. If |r| > 1 the terms grow quickly, and if |r| < 1 they shrink towards zero.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for anything that is repeatedly multiplied by the same factor: doubling, halving, interest, bouncing balls.
assumptions: the ratio between consecutive terms is constant

example.story: The sequence 3, 6, 12, 24, ... doubles each time. What is the 10th term?

formulas.name: Geometric series sum

variables.name: sum of the first n terms
variables.description: a₁ + a₁r + ... + a₁rⁿ⁻¹.

variables.name: first term
variables.description: The first term.

variables.name: common ratio
variables.description: The multiplier between terms. It must not be 1.

variables.name: number of terms
variables.description: How many terms are added.

formulas.explanation: Call the sum S. Multiplying S by r shifts every term one place along, so S - rS leaves only the first term minus the term after the last: S(1 - r) = a₁(1 - rⁿ). Dividing by 1 - r gives the formula.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to total a fixed number of terms that grow or shrink by a constant factor, such as savings plans or repeated doubling.
assumptions: r is not 1 (if r = 1 the sum is simply n a₁)

example.story: One grain of rice goes on the first square of a chessboard, two on the second, four on the third, and so on. How many grains are on the first 10 squares?

formulas.name: Infinite geometric series

variables.name: sum to infinity
variables.description: The limit of the partial sums as the number of terms grows without end.

variables.name: first term
variables.description: The first term.

variables.name: common ratio
variables.description: The multiplier between terms, strictly between -1 and 1.

formulas.explanation: When |r| < 1, the term rⁿ in the finite sum formula shrinks to zero as n grows. The partial sums then settle down to a₁/(1 - r). An infinite number of terms can add up to a finite total because the terms get small fast enough.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for repeating decimals, bouncing ball distances and any process that continues forever with a shrinking factor.
assumptions: |r| < 1, otherwise the series has no finite sum

example.story: Find the sum of 6 + 2 + 2/3 + 2/9 + ... continuing forever.

formulas.name: Product rule for exponents

variables.name: base
variables.description: The number being raised to a power. Positive here so that any real exponent is allowed.

variables.name: first exponent
variables.description: Any real exponent.

variables.name: second exponent
variables.description: Any real exponent.

formulas.explanation: a^m means m copies of a multiplied together, and a^n means n copies. Multiplying them puts m + n copies side by side. The rule keeps working for negative and fractional exponents, which is why those are defined the way they are.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to simplify products of powers with the same base.

example.story: Simplify 2³ × 2⁴.

formulas.name: Quotient rule for exponents

variables.name: base
variables.description: The number being raised to a power. Positive here so that any real exponent is allowed.

variables.name: exponent on top
variables.description: Any real exponent.

variables.name: exponent below
variables.description: Any real exponent.

formulas.explanation: Dividing cancels n of the m copies of a, leaving m - n copies. When m = n this gives a⁰ = 1, which is why any non-zero number to the power zero equals 1.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to simplify fractions of powers with the same base.
assumptions: same base on top and bottom

example.story: Simplify 5⁶ / 5⁴.

formulas.name: Power of a power

variables.name: base
variables.description: The number being raised to a power. Positive here so that any real exponent is allowed.

variables.name: inner exponent
variables.description: Any real exponent.

variables.name: outer exponent
variables.description: Any real exponent.

formulas.explanation: Raising a^m to the power n means multiplying n copies of a^m, each containing m copies of a. That is m times n copies of a in total, so the exponents multiply.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to simplify nested powers such as (x²)³.

example.story: Simplify (3²)³.

formulas.name: Negative exponent

variables.name: base
variables.description: Any positive number (any non-zero number for whole n).

variables.name: exponent
variables.description: Any real exponent.

formulas.explanation: A negative exponent means take the reciprocal. It follows from the quotient rule: a⁰ / aⁿ = a⁰⁻ⁿ = a⁻ⁿ, and a⁰ = 1. So 2⁻³ is one over 2³.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to rewrite fractions as powers (for differentiation, for example) or to make negative exponents positive.

example.story: Write 2⁻³ as a decimal.

formulas.name: Fractional exponent

variables.name: base
variables.description: A positive number.

variables.name: numerator
variables.description: The power to raise the root to.

variables.name: denominator
variables.description: Which root to take (2 for square root, 3 for cube root).

formulas.explanation: The denominator of a fractional exponent is a root and the numerator is a power. This is forced by the power rule: (a^(1/n))ⁿ = a¹ = a, so a^(1/n) must be the nth root of a. Taking the root first usually keeps the numbers small.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to evaluate powers like 8^(2/3) by hand, or to rewrite roots as powers before differentiating.
assumptions: a > 0 (odd roots of negative numbers need care)

example.story: Evaluate 8^(2/3) without a calculator.

formulas.name: Logarithm

variables.name: logarithm
variables.description: The power you must raise b to in order to get x.

variables.name: argument
variables.description: The number whose logarithm is taken. It must be positive.

variables.name: base
variables.description: The base of the logarithm: positive and not 1 (10 and e are common).

formulas.explanation: A logarithm answers the question: to which power must I raise b to get x? So log₂ 8 = 3 because 2³ = 8. Logarithms undo exponentials, which makes them the tool for solving equations where the unknown is in an exponent.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it whenever the unknown sits in an exponent, for example to find how long it takes for an amount to double.

example.story: Solve log₂ x = 5.

formulas.name: Logarithm of a product
formulas.equation: log(x*y, b) = log(x, b) + log(y, b)

variables.name: first number
variables.description: A positive number.

variables.name: second number
variables.description: A positive number.

variables.name: base
variables.description: Positive and not 1.

formulas.explanation: Logarithms are exponents, and when you multiply powers of the same base the exponents add. So the log of a product is the sum of the logs. This is why slide rules and log tables could turn multiplication into addition.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to split up or combine logarithms when simplifying or solving equations.

example.story: Check the rule with base 2, x = 8 and y = 4.

formulas.name: Logarithm of a quotient
formulas.equation: log(x / y, b) = log(x, b) - log(y, b)

variables.name: numerator
variables.description: A positive number.

variables.name: denominator
variables.description: A positive number.

variables.name: base
variables.description: Positive and not 1.

formulas.explanation: Dividing powers of the same base subtracts the exponents, so the log of a quotient is the difference of the logs. A useful special case is log(1/y) = -log y.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to simplify logarithms of fractions, for example in decibel and pH calculations.

example.story: Check the rule with base 10, x = 1000 and y = 10.

formulas.name: Logarithm of a power

variables.name: number
variables.description: A positive number.

variables.name: exponent
variables.description: Any real exponent.

variables.name: base
variables.description: Positive and not 1.

formulas.explanation: Raising x to the power k multiplies its exponent (its logarithm) by k. This rule brings an exponent down in front, which is the key step in solving equations like 2ˣ = 10.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to solve exponential equations: take logs of both sides and bring the unknown exponent down.

example.story: Check the rule with base 10, x = 100 and k = 3.

formulas.name: Change of base for logarithms

variables.name: argument
variables.description: A positive number.

variables.name: base
variables.description: Positive and not 1.

formulas.explanation: A logarithm in any base can be written using natural logs (or logs in any other common base). If y = log_b x then bʸ = x; taking ln of both sides gives y ln b = ln x. Dividing by ln b finishes the proof.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when your calculator only has ln and log, or to compare logarithms in different bases.

example.story: Find log₂ 10 using natural logarithms.

formulas.name: Percentage change

variables.name: percentage change
variables.description: Positive for an increase, negative for a decrease.

variables.name: new value
variables.description: The value after the change.

variables.name: original value
variables.description: The value before the change. It must not be zero.

formulas.explanation: The change is always compared with the original value, not the new one. Divide the change by the original, then multiply by 100 to turn the fraction into a percentage. A fall of 50 % followed by a rise of 50 % does not get you back to the start, because the second percentage is of a smaller number.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to describe price rises, discounts, population changes or the error of a measurement.

example.story: A concert ticket went up from 80 to 92. What is the percentage increase?

formulas.name: Percentage of an amount

variables.name: part
variables.description: The amount that is p percent of the whole.

variables.name: percentage
variables.description: The percentage.

variables.name: whole
variables.description: The amount the percentage is taken of.

formulas.explanation: Per cent means per hundred, so p % is the fraction p/100. Multiplying the whole by that fraction gives the part. Rearranged, p = 100 A / B tells you what percentage one amount is of another.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find a percentage of something, or what percentage one number is of another.

example.story: A student scores 45 out of 250 points on a long test. What percentage is that?

formulas.name: Percentage increase or decrease (multiplier)

variables.name: new value
variables.description: The value after the change.

variables.name: original value
variables.description: The value before the change.

variables.name: percentage change
variables.description: Positive for an increase, negative for a decrease.

formulas.explanation: Increasing by p % is the same as multiplying by the multiplier 1 + p/100, for example 1.2 for a 20 % rise or 0.85 for a 15 % fall. Solving for the original value (dividing by the multiplier) is called a reverse percentage problem.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to apply a percentage change in one step, or to find the original price before a rise or discount.

example.story: After a 20 % price rise a jacket costs 66. What did it cost before?

formulas.name: Exponential growth by a fixed percentage

variables.name: amount after t periods
variables.description: The value after growing for t periods.

variables.name: starting amount
variables.description: The value at the start.

variables.name: growth rate per period
variables.description: As a decimal, so 2.5 % is 0.025.

variables.name: number of periods
variables.description: How many periods (years, months, ...) pass.

formulas.explanation: Growing by r each period means multiplying by 1 + r each period. After t periods you have multiplied by that factor t times. Unlike linear growth, the increase gets bigger every period because it is a percentage of an ever larger amount.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for populations, prices with inflation, savings and anything else that grows by the same percentage each period.

example.story: A town of 12 000 people grows by 2.5 % per year. How many people live there after 8 years?

formulas.name: Exponential decay by a fixed percentage

variables.name: amount after t periods
variables.description: The value after shrinking for t periods.

variables.name: starting amount
variables.description: The value at the start.

variables.name: decay rate per period
variables.description: As a decimal, so 15 % is 0.15.

variables.name: number of periods
variables.description: How many periods pass.

formulas.explanation: Losing r each period means keeping 1 - r of what was there, so you multiply by 1 - r every period. The amount never reaches zero but keeps shrinking by the same fraction. To find when it falls to a target value, take logarithms.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for depreciation, cooling-like processes described by a percentage, or medicine leaving the body at a fixed rate per hour.

example.story: A car worth 20 000 loses 15 % of its value every year. After how many years is it worth 10 000?

formulas.name: Continuous exponential growth

variables.name: amount at time t
variables.description: The value after time t.

variables.name: starting amount
variables.description: The value at t = 0.

variables.name: growth constant
variables.description: Rate per unit of time; negative for decay. Use the same time unit as t.

variables.name: time
variables.description: Elapsed time, in the same unit that k is measured per.

formulas.explanation: When something grows at a rate proportional to its current size, the solution of dN/dt = kN is N₀e^(kt). The constant e appears because growth is happening all the time, not in steps. A positive k means growth and a negative k means decay.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for bacteria, continuous compounding, and any model where the rate of change is proportional to the amount.
assumptions: the rate of change is proportional to the amount

example.story: A culture starts with 500 bacteria and grows with k = 0.4 per hour. How many are there after 5 hours?

formulas.name: Doubling time

variables.name: doubling time
variables.description: The time it takes for the amount to double, in the unit k is measured per.

variables.name: growth constant
variables.description: The continuous growth rate per unit of time.

formulas.explanation: Doubling means e^(kT) = 2. Taking natural logs gives kT = ln 2, so T = ln 2 / k ≈ 0.693/k. Every doubling time the amount doubles again, whatever it is at the start.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to get a feel for how fast exponential growth is, or to find the growth constant from a known doubling time.
assumptions: continuous exponential growth with constant k

example.story: A population grows continuously with k = 0.04 per year. How long does it take to double?

formulas.name: Direct proportion

variables.name: dependent quantity
variables.description: The quantity that changes in proportion to x.

variables.name: constant of proportionality
variables.description: The fixed ratio y / x.

variables.name: independent quantity
variables.description: The quantity you change.

formulas.explanation: Two quantities are directly proportional when their ratio is always the same. Double x and y doubles; the graph is a straight line through the origin with gradient k. Find k from one known pair, then use it for any other.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for recipes, exchange rates, cost per item, and many physical laws where one quantity is proportional to another.
assumptions: y is zero when x is zero

example.story: y is directly proportional to x, and y = 12 when x = 4. Find the constant k.

formulas.name: Inverse proportion

variables.name: dependent quantity
variables.description: The quantity that changes inversely with x.

variables.name: constant of proportionality
variables.description: The fixed product x times y.

variables.name: independent quantity
variables.description: The quantity you change. It must not be zero.

formulas.explanation: Two quantities are inversely proportional when their product is always the same. Doubling x halves y, and the graph is a hyperbola. The constant k equals any known x times its y.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for problems like workers and time, speed and travel time, or pressure and volume at constant temperature.

example.story: 6 painters take 10 days to paint a school, so k = 60 painter-days. How long would 4 painters take?

formulas.name: Distance between two points

variables.name: distance
variables.description: The straight-line distance between the points.

variables.name: x of second point
variables.description: x coordinate of the second point.

variables.name: x of first point
variables.description: x coordinate of the first point.

variables.name: y of second point
variables.description: y coordinate of the second point.

variables.name: y of first point
variables.description: y coordinate of the first point.

formulas.explanation: The horizontal and vertical gaps between two points form the two short sides of a right-angled triangle. The distance between the points is the hypotenuse, so Pythagoras' theorem gives it directly. The order of the points does not matter because the gaps are squared.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find lengths of line segments, radii of circles, or to check whether a triangle is isosceles.
assumptions: flat (Cartesian) coordinates with equal scales on both axes

example.story: How far apart are the points (1, 2) and (7, 10)?

formulas.name: Midpoint of a line segment

variables.name: midpoint coordinate
variables.description: The coordinate of the midpoint.

variables.name: first endpoint coordinate
variables.description: The same coordinate of the first endpoint.

variables.name: second endpoint coordinate
variables.description: The same coordinate of the second endpoint.

formulas.explanation: The midpoint is halfway along a segment, so each of its coordinates is the average of the endpoints' coordinates. Apply the formula once for x and once for y (and once more for z in 3D).
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the centre of a circle from a diameter, or to bisect a line segment.

example.story: A diameter of a circle runs from x = -3 to x = 9 along the x axis. Where is the centre?

formulas.name: Gradient of a line through two points

variables.name: gradient
variables.description: The slope: how much y goes up for each step of 1 in x.

variables.name: y of second point
variables.description: y coordinate of the second point.

variables.name: y of first point
variables.description: y coordinate of the first point.

variables.name: x of second point
variables.description: x coordinate of the second point.

variables.name: x of first point
variables.description: x coordinate of the first point.

formulas.explanation: The gradient is rise over run: the change in y divided by the change in x. A positive gradient slopes up to the right, a negative one slopes down, and a vertical line has no gradient because the run is zero.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the slope of a line, a rate of change from a graph, or as the first step to the equation of a line.
assumptions: x₂ ≠ x₁ (the line is not vertical)

example.story: Find the gradient of the line through (2, 3) and (6, 11).

formulas.name: Equation of a straight line (slope-intercept form)

variables.name: y coordinate
variables.description: The height of the line at x.

variables.name: gradient
variables.description: The slope of the line.

variables.name: x coordinate
variables.description: Any position along the horizontal axis.

variables.name: y-intercept
variables.description: Where the line crosses the y axis (the value of y when x = 0).

formulas.explanation: Every non-vertical straight line can be written as y = mx + c. Start at height c on the y axis and climb m units for every unit you move right. Many textbooks write y = ax + b or y = mx + b for the same thing.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to draw a line from its equation, to read off slope and intercept, or to find where a line reaches a given height.

example.story: On the line y = 2x - 1, at which x does y equal 9?

formulas.name: Equation of a straight line (point-slope form)

variables.name: y coordinate
variables.description: The height of the line at x.

variables.name: y of known point
variables.description: y coordinate of a point on the line.

variables.name: gradient
variables.description: The slope of the line.

variables.name: x coordinate
variables.description: Any position along the horizontal axis.

variables.name: x of known point
variables.description: x coordinate of a point on the line.

formulas.explanation: If a line passes through (x₁, y₁) with gradient m, then for any other point on it the rise y - y₁ is m times the run x - x₁. That is just the gradient formula rearranged. It is the quickest way to write down a line when you know one point and the slope.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the equation of a tangent or normal, or of any line through a known point with a known slope.

example.story: A line has gradient 3 and passes through (2, 5). What is y when x = 4?

formulas.name: Equation of a straight line (intercept form)

variables.name: x coordinate
variables.description: Any position along the horizontal axis.

variables.name: x-intercept
variables.description: Where the line crosses the x axis. Not zero.

variables.name: y coordinate
variables.description: The height of the line at x.

variables.name: y-intercept
variables.description: Where the line crosses the y axis. Not zero.

formulas.explanation: Putting y = 0 gives x = a and putting x = 0 gives y = b, so the line passes through (a, 0) and (0, b). This form shows both intercepts at a glance and makes the line easy to sketch.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when you know where a line crosses both axes, for example budget lines in economics.
assumptions: the line does not pass through the origin and is not parallel to an axis

example.story: A line crosses the axes at (4, 0) and (0, 6). What is y when x = 2?

formulas.name: Equation of a circle

variables.name: x coordinate
variables.description: x of a point on the circle.

variables.name: x of centre
variables.description: x coordinate of the centre.

variables.name: y coordinate
variables.description: y of a point on the circle.

variables.name: y of centre
variables.description: y coordinate of the centre.

variables.name: radius
variables.description: Distance from the centre to the circle.

formulas.explanation: A circle is the set of points at distance r from its centre (a, b). Writing that distance with the distance formula and squaring both sides gives this equation. A point is inside the circle when the left side is less than r².
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the equation of a circle, check whether a point lies on it, or find intersections with lines.

example.story: A circle has centre (3, -2) and passes through (6, 2). What is its radius?

formulas.name: Gradients of perpendicular lines

variables.name: gradient of first line
variables.description: Slope of one line (not zero).

variables.name: gradient of second line
variables.description: Slope of the line at right angles to it.

formulas.explanation: Rotating a line by 90 degrees turns a run of 1 and a rise of m into a run of -m and a rise of 1, so the new gradient is -1/m. Multiplying the two gradients therefore always gives -1. Parallel lines, by contrast, have equal gradients.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the equation of a normal to a curve, a perpendicular bisector, or to test whether two lines meet at right angles.
assumptions: neither line is horizontal or vertical

example.story: A line has gradient 2/3. What is the gradient of a line perpendicular to it?
